1:
John Gill begins with the missing adjective: good is not in the text but is rightly supplied, as three old versions supply it, since not any name is preferable to riches—with some a name turns to reproach—but a good name among good men. Adam Clarke notes the same supplement in four versions and observes that the Hebrew uses it much as we do in saying a man has got a name; character supports a man in many circumstances, and there are rich men who have none, so a man of credit’s word goes farther than their riches. Matthew Henry counts two things preferred to wealth, being well spoken of and well beloved, and presses the comparison: great riches bring great cares and add no real value, a fool and a knave may have them, and while riches relieve the bodily wants of others a good name recommends religion to them. Charles Ellicott notes that the favour of the second clause may mean the grace that wins love or the love it wins; John Wesley, a good report among good men with the hearty kindness attending it.

On the rich and poor meeting, the readings run from social to eschatological. Gill offers three senses—a hostile meeting, with contempt on one side and envy on the other; a dependence, neither able to say it has no need of the other; or an exchange of places, the poor going uphill and the rich down, and so meeting in the passage. Clarke works out the economics: the poor include all the labouring classes, and without them the rich could not be supplied, while without the rich the poor could find no vent for their labour, their spare time going to the superfluities the rich consume, and paid for by them; God, he says, in effect lays the destitute at the rich man’s door. Keil and Delitzsch make the meeting itself God’s ordinance and a school of virtue, where the lowly serve the exalted and the exalted the lowly. Henry adds the two places where they meet on level terms, the bar of justice, where both are guilty, and the throne of grace, where the poor are as welcome; there is one heaven for poor saints and one hell for rich sinners. Ellicott has them thrown together to aid one another as sons of one Father; Wesley warns that neither can despise or grudge at the other without reflecting on God.

The prudent man’s foresight draws examples. Henry has him aware when he enters a temptation and putting on his armour, taking warning as the clouds gather, and cites the flood foreseen and the famine provided against; the simple, who believe every word that flatters them, will believe none that warns them, and nothing is so fatal to souls. Ellicott adds the houses shut against the destroying angel and the Christians withdrawn before a city’s fall. Keil and Delitzsch supply plainer pictures, a decaying house about to fall or a storm bringing a flood, and note that this group of proverbs runs to the seventh verse, closing as the last did with a saying about rich and poor. Clarke draws a providence from it: God has denied man knowledge of the future but given hope and prudence instead, the one anticipating good and the other finding means to secure it, while the simple run on in hope with no prudence to regulate it. Gill and Wesley make the hiding a retreat to God. The verse that follows is disputed in construction. Ellicott and Gill report the rendering that makes the fear of the Lord itself the reward of humility, which Keil and Delitzsch say all the old interpreters took, though some read two virtues joined without a connective; Henry keeps the received sense and finds religion summed up in the pair, since where the fear of God is there will be humility.
5:
The thorns and snares are read as the natural fruit of a crooked course. Keil and Delitzsch admit the etymology of both nouns is unverified though the meaning stands fast, and picture the perverse man driving his winding way to match his habit of mind, into thorns that entangle and snares that bring him down unawares. Matthew Henry divides them—thorns of grief for past sins, snares that entangle in further sin—and observes that a man who makes no conscience of what he says is hampered by his imaginary liberty and tormented by his own pleasures; everything, he adds, will fret and vex the man who frets and vexes at everything. John Gill takes them for the thorns of affliction and the snares of Satan, one hedging up the way and the other catching the feet; Adam Clarke leaves them as difficulties, trials and sufferings.

The verse on training a child is the chapter’s crux, and turns on what his way means. Keil and Delitzsch reject three readings in turn—the calling he must enter, the course he must keep through life, his individual temperament—and settle on the nature of childhood as such, so that matter and manner of instruction follow the stage of life. Clarke takes the Hebrew as an initiation at the opening of the path: when the child can walk alone and choose, stop there and begin a course of instruction in the duties, dangers and blessings before him, fixing it by daily inculcation till the impression is indelible, then leading him to practice by degrees so slow as to be imperceptible, till it becomes a rooted habit. He notes that the verb also means to dedicate, as things are consecrated to God, and would have the child given to God first and disciplined as his, entrusted to a parent. Henry warns against training in the way the child would go, since a corrupt heart’s bias draws that way, and would have them trained as soldiers taught to handle arms and keep rank, yet fed like nurslings, little and often. He and Clarke reach one image by different roads—the vessel keeps the savour it was first seasoned with, which Clarke finds in a Latin poet’s line on the odour a new jar keeps from its first wine. Henry is honest about the exceptions: many have left the way they were trained in, Solomon among them, though early training may be the means of recovery. Gill reads the clause as by the mouth of his way, from the moment the child can speak; John Wesley only qualifies the promise, that he will not depart from it easily or ordinarily.

The two sayings that follow are read as description, not approval—though not by all. Gill says the rich usurp a dominion and use it rigorously, though where they rule well it is commendable; Clarke says the arrangement is in the order of God and may be a blessing to both. Keil and Delitzsch call it the course of the world, note that there are many poor to one rich and that in the East rule lies generally in one hand, and that debt brings a slavish dependence naturally. Henry sets the verse against the earlier one about rich and poor meeting: in the things of this life the difference is great, the rich ruling more than becomes them, unlike God, who though great despises none, and the borrower obliged to beg for patience—some selling liberty to gratify luxury. On the sower Henry adds that those who create trouble for others prepare it for themselves, and a rod of authority turned into a rod of anger will be broken. Clarke asks whether a man who sows thistle seed can look for wheat. Charles Ellicott glosses the vanity as calamity and has the oppressor suffer in his turn the punishment he inflicted, as two empires did.
9:
Matthew Henry reads the bountiful eye closely: the opposite of the evil eye and the same as the single eye, an eye that seeks out objects of charity besides those that offer themselves, that is moved to compassion at the sight of want, and that gives a pleasant look with the alms, which makes them doubly acceptable. He is as exact on the second clause—the man gives of his bread, the bread appointed for his own eating, and would rather abridge himself than see the poor perish, yet gives of it and not all of it, so the poor share with his own family. Adam Clarke looks behind the organ: the bountiful eye means the bountiful heart, since the heart looks through the eye, and the merciful heart is blessed even when the hand has little to give. Keil and Delitzsch set the phrase against its opposite, the evil-eyed and ungracious man, note the rabbinic term for such kindness, and observe that the Greek adds a couplet here which the Hebrew lacks. John Gill and John Wesley keep to the plain description of a man who looks about for proper objects and on their misery with compassion.

The scorner draws the sharpest character-sketch. Keil and Delitzsch describe the man found in a circle of friends who treats religious questions without respect, moral questions frivolously and serious things jestingly, and who out of a passion for witticism and love of anecdote sets himself above the duty of reverence; chase him away, and the dispeace goes out with him. They add that the last noun always means disgrace as something that happens, not the injury others take from him. Henry reports a rendering that makes him the evil interpreter, construing everything into the worst, and concludes that whoever would secure the peace must exclude him. Gill widens the expulsion to the family and the church, recalling the mocker turned out of the patriarch’s house, and rejects the reading that makes the scorner the corrupt nature within, since that stays with a man as long as he lives and can be weakened but not cast out.

The verse on the pure heart is grammatically the hardest, and Keil and Delitzsch rule out three constructions: that a man loves with a pure heart; that his lips will be gracious because he loves purity, since between the two there is a moral relation but no necessary sequence; and that he loves both purity and grace on his own lips, which would sound less like a virtue than self-complacency. The rendering they most approve makes it simply that a man with a true heart and amiable speech has the king for his friend. Charles Ellicott agrees, glossing the second clause as one who loves truth and can speak it pleasantly. Henry draws the portrait of a man fit for public business, honest and free of dissimulation, able to deliver his sentiments in language as clean and smooth as his spirit, and notes that both the old courts had an officer styled the king’s friend; some, he adds, understand the King of kings, who befriends the man in whose spirit is no guile. Clarke takes it that way outright, with a shrewd reason for the earthly sense too: no class of men values uprightness more than kings, since none need it so much in their servants. Gill notes that some versions turn the verse round: God loves pure hearts. On the last saying, Gill and Clarke take the eyes for providence and instance the preservation of the Scriptures against those who would have destroyed them, Clarke adding the ancient authors preserved with them; Keil and Delitzsch argue that knowledge stands by metonymy for men of knowledge, since God’s eyes cannot keep themselves by a rule; Henry and Wesley say the same, that he preserves faithful witnesses and turns the counsels of treacherous men to their own confusion.
13:
The sluggard’s lion is treated as comedy with a sting. Keil and Delitzsch note that his work would take him into the open country, and that the strong word he chooses for being murdered is picked to make the pretence ridiculously hyperbolical; they observe too that he says it flatly, with no perhaps and no lest. Matthew Henry makes the point morally: a man with no love for his business will never want excuses, and multitudes are ruined by sloth while always having something to say for themselves, so ingenious are men at cheating their own souls. He does not himself believe it, Henry adds, he only says it to those who call him up—and while he talks of a lion in the street he never considers the roaring lion nearer home, or the slothfulness that is killing him. Adam Clarke puts it as a diagnosis: why does he say so? Because he is a slothful man; remove the sloth and the imaginary dangers vanish. John Gill answers from natural history, that lions walk in woods and mountains, not the streets of towns; Charles Ellicott, that no excuse is too absurd for such a man.

The pit dug for the unwary is read by all of them as a trap with a moral mechanism. Gill takes the figure from beasts caught in a pit; Keil and Delitzsch make it a snare-pit into which a man is enticed by wanton words, and add that one in fellowship with God is armed against the siren voice, while the man already under divine indignation, which punishes evil with evil, goes in. Henry says the same more bluntly: those who abandon themselves to the sin prove themselves abandoned by God, who withdraws the bridle of restraining grace to punish them for other sins—so a man is not to value himself on standing well with such women when it only proclaims him under wrath. Clarke reaches for the classics, setting beside the verse the descent in Virgil, where the way down lies smooth and the gate stands open night and day, but to climb back to the upper air is the labour and the long unconquerable pain. John Wesley reduces the mouth to fair and flattering speeches.

What the child’s bound-in folly is divides them three ways. Gill and Henry take it for original corruption—sin brought into the world with the child and not merely found in the heart but tied to it, cleaving, as Henry says, like a scion to the stock it is grafted into, a knot between the soul and sin. Keil and Delitzsch take something lighter, pleasure in stupid tricks and silly sport, the portion of children as such, which education drives out only when unindulgently severe; they quote a comic poet to the effect that the man who is not flogged is not educated, and note a mangled version in which the folly makes the child’s understanding fly away. Ellicott takes it for self-will, and says children have to be taught to yield their wills to others. Henry adds that under the correction we must stroke down folly and kiss the rod. On the last verse the construction is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch canvass the readings, including one referring the two participles to two classes of men rather than one, and object that the intended antithesis then fails; Ellicott makes the oppressor thereby a giver to the rich, since he must disgorge his prey to someone stronger and be impoverished himself. Henry sees the two habits in one man, who will not relieve the poor but entertains the rich, from vainglory or from policy—and remarks that many have been beggared by a foolish generosity but never any by a prudent charity. Clarke and Wesley put it plainly, that a man robs the poor to make presents to those who do not need them.
17:
All of them notice the book changing here. John Gill calls it a new division, in another style, by way of exhortation and instruction, directed to particular persons. Keil and Delitzsch are precise about the boundary: what precedes is the Proverbs of Solomon and what follows the Words of the Wise, so these five verses are a prologue and not an epilogue, written after the collection they preface, which is why the verbs are perfects. Charles Ellicott infers from the plural noun that the section contains proverbs by others than Solomon, however they came to be gathered. Matthew Henry marks a change of manner rather than of authorship: hitherto the sense was mostly comprised in one verse and the application left to the reader, but from here the address is direct and the thought drawn out—wisdom, he says, tries variety of methods with us lest we be cloyed with any one. He turns it on preachers: it is not enough to preach before hearers, one must preach to them, nor enough to preach to all in general without addressing particular persons; and the ear will not serve without the heart.

Adam Clarke lays the passage out as a scheme, taking in turn the exhortation, the profit of hearing, and the end the instruction serves. The words are to be heard with humility and deep attention, then treasured, then digested until the hearer gains an experimental knowledge and can speak of them persuasively. Ellicott would render the clause about the lips as a condition, if they dwell constantly there, and makes them a watch on its door, teaching a man what to say in difficulty and how to speak without fear even before kings. Gill reads the same clause of the inmost recesses, recalling the roll that was honey for sweetness in the prophet’s belly; John Wesley takes the fitting for an ability to discourse profitably of them. On the day of the teaching Ellicott hears an emphasis, that a message general in form is addressed to each soul; Henry hears a warning, that the light is with us only a little while, and what is made known today may before tomorrow be hidden from a man who does not improve his day.

The word they all stop at is the adjective in the twentieth verse, which can be read as a numeral. Clarke sets out the possibilities without hiding his impatience: the three books ascribed to Solomon; the three divisions of the sacred books; three intellectual sciences, though Solomon’s natural philosophy is lost; the three senses of Scripture later readers found. Since thrice is used as seven is, a certain number for an uncertain, he thinks it may only mean the writing was often repeated—but concludes it is safer to take the other sense, of excellent and princely things, such as become a king to speak. Gill goes through the same list independently, objects to the reading that makes it the three divisions of the canon since part of those writings did not then exist, and settles on the same rendering on three named authorities. Henry presses the dignity of the same word: these are not jocular proverbs to pass the time but princely things, fit for kings to speak and senates to hear, which will not only make us knowing but enable us to advise others. On the last verse Clarke says the words of truth are not of dubious interpretation and are to be experimentally understood, so the believer has the witness in himself and can meet inquiry with the speediest and most distinct answer; Ellicott, calling his own rendering doubtful, takes the point to be that the scholar is taught not for his own profit alone but that he may teach others; Gill and Wesley add only that the words come from the God of truth and the learner should be able to give a solid answer.
22:
Matthew Henry notices the anticlimax: after so solemn a preface one would expect something new and surprising, and instead comes a plain but very needful caution against oppressing the poor. He piles up the absurdity of it—to squeeze with our power those we should water with our bounty, to add affliction to the afflicted, and to give judgment against them, which patronises the robbery and is as bad as robbing them ourselves. Rich men will not let themselves be wronged; poor men cannot help it, which is why the wrong is worse: to rob a man because he is helpless is not merely base and cowardly but unnatural, and proves men worse than beasts. John Gill makes the same point from the law courts, that the poor man cannot go to law with the man who has injured him, which emboldens the injurer; and he offers a second reading of the particle, making the poverty a concession rather than a reason—though he is poor, let that be no inducement. Adam Clarke and Charles Ellicott supply the setting: the gate was where business was done and justice administered, courts being held at the city gates in the East, and Ellicott points to a surviving title in which a government is still named from a gate. John Wesley reduces the second clause to oppression under pretence of justice.

The threat that follows is read as a change of adversary. Gill has it that if counsel at the bar will not plead for them God will, and if the judges on the bench will not do them justice he will—so that woe is to the man against whom the Lord pleads. Clarke puts it in a sentence: the oppressor will have God, and not the poor man, to deal with. Henry works both halves, the oppressed finding a powerful patron and the oppressor a just avenger, who will spoil the souls of those that spoil them, so that a man who robs the poor is found in the end the murderer of himself. Keil and Delitzsch note the form rather than the force, that this verse and the one before make a quatrain, as the next pair does.

On choosing friends the commentators agree and differ only in emphasis. Henry rests it on the law of friendship, that we accommodate ourselves to those we are tied to, so that a man easily provoked and apt to resent affronts is not fit to be chosen: he will be angry with us, which will be our trouble, and will expect us to be angry with others, which will be our sin. Gill adds the distinction between civility and intimacy—a man should be courteous to all and cautious whom he admits to his bosom. Keil and Delitzsch supply the idiom, that the angry man is named a master of anger as a covetous man is a master of appetite, the second word being stronger, a hot-head of the highest degree. On the reason given, Clarke states the principle broadly, that spirit has a wonderful and unaccountable influence upon spirit, so that from those we keep company with we acquire habits, imbibe their temper and walk in their steps. Henry sharpens it: our corrupt hearts have so much tinder in them that it is dangerous to converse with men who throw about the sparks of their passion—and he observes what the warning does not say, that we may get ill language or a broken head, but the worse thing, that we may imitate the man to humour him and so contract the habit. Gill instances how quickly evil is learned, since men are readier to copy what is bad than what is good, and remarks that men naturally mild have been made fierce by living among the cruel. Ellicott glosses the snare to the soul simply as the loss of life.
26:
The warning against suretyship is given a legal and a moral edge. Matthew Henry begins with the company: men of broken fortunes will urge their friends to be bound for them, so as to cheat their neighbours a little longer and do the more damage at the end to those who gave them credit. He then divides the debtors: a man disabled by providence deserves pity and help, but one who binds himself knowing he has nothing to pay with picks his neighbour’s pocket, and may thank himself if the law takes the bed from under him—which, Henry notes, might legally be taken as a pledge, though a man with nothing else to offer ought rather to have been relieved. John Gill grades the offence: weakness to be surety when a man knows he cannot pay, wickedness to engage for a debt he knows he cannot answer, since that deceives the creditor. Adam Clarke asks bluntly whether giving security for more than one is worth is not a fraud on the face of it, and observes that a creditor will not pursue a debtor he knows to be worth nothing but will sue the surety. Charles Ellicott adds the law behind the bed: a garment taken in pledge had to be returned before sundown for a poor man to sleep in, and the merciful provision was evidently evaded.

The landmark draws the most interesting convergence. Keil and Delitzsch call its removal a double transgression, the boundary being made sacred by its antiquity, and note a variant which one rabbi took of those brought up out of bondage and another of the poor, rising being a polite word for coming down in the world. Henry treats the stones as standing witnesses to every man’s right, whose removal breeds wars and endless disputes and entails fraud on posterity, and extends the principle to settled usages, which should not be altered under pretence of altering for the better. Clarke gives the practical fraud—ploughing a neighbouring field and shifting the stones a little further in—and the antiquarian evidence, a Latin poet on the god who presided over boundaries, with the owners of both fields bringing garlands and libations, since without that witness every field would be matter of litigation. Both then face the application to religion, and answer alike but not identically: Gill allows doctrines settled by Christ and the apostles the name of ancient landmarks but not those of the fathers who followed, as fallible men; Clarke forbids new dogmas or rites not clearly laid down in Scripture, but insists that calling a church back to doctrines it has lost sight of is not removing a landmark, whatever some have falsely asserted.

The chapter ends on the diligent man, and they are struck chiefly by how rare he is. Henry reads the question as an intimation that one will not see many such, so epidemical are dulness and sloth, and praises the man who lays himself out to get business even in a narrow sphere, is uneasy when he has none, and knows how to bring a deal of business into a little compass. Gill agrees that such a man is not very common, and that having found one you may foresee without any spirit of prophecy that he will rise. Keil and Delitzsch define his skill as mastery of a calling by intelligence and not mere external ability, and read the promise as an entitlement: he can enter the service of kings and need not enter that of obscure men. Clarke glosses the last word as obscure persons of no repute, and sums the proverb up: every active man will be at once independent and respectable. Ellicott and John Wesley make the standing an attendance on princes, and Henry turns the saying upwards at the last: the man diligent in the business of religion shall stand before the King of kings.
